title: Ukraine raises death toll from Zaporizhia aid centre strike above 50
summary: Rescuers say Monday's bombing of a village aid site is among the deadliest Russian attacks this year, with dozens still feared under the rubble.
body:
Ukraine has raised the death toll from a Russian strike on an aid distribution centre in the Zaporizhia region to more than 50, calling it one of the deadliest attacks of the year.

Emergency crews said Friday that more bodies had been recovered from the ruins in the village of Komyshuvakha after Monday's raid. The acting regional governor put the toll at 53 as searchers worked into a fifth day. Local police earlier listed dozens of people as missing and warned that many may still lie trapped under debris.

Ukrainian officials say Russian aircraft bombed a former school near the front that civilians used for weekly aid handouts. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a first blast was followed by a second wave aimed at the underground shelter where people had taken cover, causing most of the destruction. Police officers and rescue workers were among the dead.

DNA testing is being used to identify remains while further Russian fire continues to endanger the rescue effort. The United Nations human rights mission in Ukraine said the strike was likely a breach of international law. Kyiv cast the attack as proof that Moscow will not halt the fighting even after short local pauses elsewhere along the line.

The raid came a day after a brief ceasefire ended in a Russian occupied city further south. For families still waiting on names and for communities that rely on aid points near the front, the rising toll underlines how civilian supply lines remain exposed in a war now stretching toward its fifth year.

title: Europe fears a US security deal with Russia that weakens NATO
summary: Officials worry Washington could strike terms with Moscow that restore a Russian sphere of influence and undercut allied security guarantees.
body:
European governments are sounding the alarm over reports that Washington is exploring a security arrangement with Moscow that allies fear could hollow out NATO and hand Russia a renewed sphere of influence.

Public briefings from European officials describe anxiety that any bilateral understanding between the United States and Russia might trade Ukrainian leverage or eastern flank guarantees for a quick diplomatic win. Capitals that have poured weapons and money into Ukraine's defence say they were not reassured by signals that the White House wants a grand bargain with the Kremlin.

The concern lands days after Democratic midterm gains, when many in Europe hoped Congress would stiffen American support. Diplomats note that foreign policy still runs chiefly through the presidency, so legislative shifts may not block a deal if the White House pursues one.

Allies are pressing for consultation before any text takes shape and for clear red lines on Ukrainian sovereignty and forward defence of NATO members. Without that, they warn, years of military aid and political unity could be spent down in a settlement that freezes the war on Moscow's preferred map.

title: Trump weighs vetoes and deals after Democrats take Congress
summary: With both chambers lost, the president says he will not spend two years only blocking bills, even as he flaunts the veto power he still holds.
body:
President Donald Trump is weighing how to govern after Democrats seized both chambers of Congress, floating cooperation even while reminding rivals that he can veto nearly anything they pass.

As midterm results confirmed a Democratic wave, Trump told an interviewer he had already taken calls from Democrats who want to work with him. He said he does not want to spend two years only striking down legislation, while stressing that the veto remains his. He later posted imagery playing on the word veto, underlining the leverage he still holds.

Democrats have secured comfortable majorities in the House and Senate on the counts reported so far, yet they lack the two thirds margins needed to override a presidential veto in either chamber. Analysts say that leaves three broad paths for the White House: veto bills, lean harder on executive orders, or cut selective deals.

Trump has already signed hundreds of executive orders across his current term, a habit that may grow if Capitol Hill turns hostile. Scholars of American politics expect stretches of gridlock, with Democrats advancing priorities they know may die on his desk and the president picking moments to bargain when he wants a win.

For markets, allies and domestic agencies, the practical question is which files invite compromise and which invite confrontation. Immigration, spending, artificial intelligence rules and foreign military authorities all sit in the contested middle. The midterms changed the arithmetic; they did not remove the veto pen.

title: US tech shares rebound after midterm AI selloff
summary: The Nasdaq climbed in Friday trade as chipmakers clawed back part of Thursday's steep losses tied to fears of slower AI growth under Democrats.
body:
United States technology shares bounced on Friday after a bruising midterm selloff that had wiped trillions from market values on worries that Democratic gains would slow the artificial intelligence boom.

The Nasdaq Composite opened more than one percent higher and kept rising in early trade, reversing part of Thursday's drop of about five and a half percent. The S&P 500 also edged up while the Dow was little changed. Chip and AI linked names that led the plunge led the repair job.

Nvidia, which had shed hundreds of billions in value after a slide of more than nine percent, jumped more than six percent at the open. AMD and Micron, both down more than seventeen percent on Thursday, posted strong double digit percentage gains in early Friday dealing. Tesla and other previously hit names showed smaller recoveries.

Investors had sold technology stocks partly because they expect a Democratic Congress to tighten rules on data centres, power use and AI buildouts. Fresh employment figures that showed a surprisingly firm hiring print added to a mixed macro picture and helped some buyers step back in.

The rebound does not erase Thursday's damage or settle the policy debate. Traders are still parsing how far new majorities will go on AI scrutiny, export controls and energy permits. For now the message from the tape is simpler: part of the panic faded once bargain hunters returned to the same chip giants that led the rout.

title: US employers add 165,000 jobs in stronger than forecast report
summary: A hiring rebound led by professional services pointed to continued strength in the American labour market after the midterm shock.
body:
United States employers added 165,000 jobs in the latest monthly report, outstripping forecasts and underscoring resilience in the American labour market even as politics and markets jolted after the midterms.

Hiring strength was led by professional services, according to the public summary of the figures, painting a firmer picture than many economists had expected. The print landed on a morning when technology shares were trying to rebound from a steep AI linked selloff and investors were hunting for signals on growth and interest rate paths.

A solid jobs number complicates simple narratives that political upheaval would immediately cool the economy. It also feeds debate at the Federal Reserve about how much room remains to adjust borrowing costs while unemployment stays contained and pay pressures evolve.

For the White House and the new Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill, the data offer a backdrop of still functioning labour demand as budget and regulatory fights begin. For workers, the headline is more direct: employers kept adding roles at a pace that beat the consensus screen.

title: Iran's chief negotiator says Americans voted no to war
summary: Parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf hailed the midterm message against the conflict as Trump again tied Republican losses to the Iran fight and higher fuel prices.
body:
Iran's chief negotiator with the United States says American voters delivered a clear no to war, after Republicans suffered heavy midterm losses that President Donald Trump partly blamed on the Iran conflict.

Parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf wrote that Americans had voted against the war and that Tehran endorsed that message. He warned that if Washington ignored its own public to serve what he called foreign paymasters, Iran's refusal would come with severe consequences.

Trump has acknowledged that the fighting and the jump in petrol prices hurt Republican candidates, while insisting he does not regret launching the campaign and saying the war ends when he decides it ends. In recent weeks he has also left open the chance of renewed all out strikes with Israel if no deal is reached.

The exchange captures the strange symmetry of the moment. Iranian officials cast the ballot box as proof that the war is unpopular in America. The White House still claims authority to continue or expand operations. Mediators and markets are left reading both the vote and the threats as they wait for the next concrete proposal or the next raid.

title: Ukraine arrests woman behind viral false conscription torture claim
summary: Officials say a staged rescue outside Kyiv fuelled a global storm over draft tactics, after a crowd stormed a suburban house on false allegations.
body:
Ukrainian authorities have arrested a woman who sparked a viral scandal by claiming men seized for conscription were being tortured in a suburban house outside Kyiv, officials say the episode was staged.

Valentyna Moloda, described as a 49 year old nurse not authorised to work as a paramedic, knelt before police at a two storey house in Petropavlivska Borshchagivka and alleged that armed captors were holding dozens of draft evaders, with at least one already dead. An ambulance marked with logos of a private firm said to have closed years earlier stood nearby as a companion livestreamed and a crowd swelled into the hundreds.

Protesters threw eggs and tomatoes, clashed with officers into the night and pushed a narrative that spread worldwide among critics of Ukraine's draft. Conscription teams are widely disliked for harsh methods, which helped the claim catch fire before facts caught up.

Officials now say the rescue was fake and prepared in advance. Ukraine's intelligence leadership said Moloda and a driver had scouted the property days earlier. Investigators argue the house was not a torture site and that the performance was built to inflame.

The affair leaves a double wound. It exposed raw anger over how men are pulled into a grinding war with Russia. It also showed how quickly an unverified livestream can shape foreign perceptions of a country fighting for survival. Courts and police will now test the fraud case while commanders still face a public that distrusts the draft.

title: Uncertainty grips Iran after US midterm shock
summary: Pro government crowds celebrate Republican losses while many Iranians fear repression will continue whatever happens next with Trump and the war.
body:
Hours after Republican losses in the US midterms became clear, crowds in Tehran burned a giant banner showing Donald Trump, JD Vance, envoy Steve Witkoff and Benjamin Netanyahu. Officials cast the vote as a rebuke of Trump's war on Iran. Supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said America's decline had sped up. State television even aired a staged mock hanging of Trump.

Away from the rallies, many Iranians describe dread rather than triumph. A Tehran journalist said people feel trapped in a strange limbo, looking to Washington and Jerusalem for change while the economy worsens and daily life grows harsher. Some fear that, with no re election race left for Trump, he could escalate again. Others think another full scale war is less likely after the ballot shock. Almost all agree the security state at home will not ease.

A rights monitor based in Oslo says Iranian authorities have executed at least 696 people this year. Residents speak of shops still open while real purchases shrink, of families debating heaters in case infrastructure is hit again, and of a prison machine that kept running through earlier fighting. A medic in central Iran argued outsiders still underestimate the Revolutionary Guard's loyalty and competence, and that a system able to absorb sanctions can also turn that force on its own people.

The mood on the street is preparation for the worst with little faith that European leaders will press the case of those still being arrested and killed. Celebrations by hardliners, one resident said, look like relief that the ruling structure has found room to survive.

title: Saudi led strike on Yemeni home kills nine relatives, family says
summary: Relatives say an October air raid destroyed a household in the war against the Houthis, renewing focus on civilian deaths in the US backed campaign.
body:
Relatives say a Saudi led air raid in October destroyed a Yemeni home and killed nine members of one family, spotlighting civilian harm in the long campaign against the Houthis.

The strike is described as part of operations that also involve US support. Families and local accounts place the dead inside a residential building rather than a clear military site, a pattern rights monitors have flagged across years of fighting in Yemen.

Riyadh and its partners cast the air war as necessary to roll back Houthi advances and protect shipping and border areas. Critics say too little is done to verify targets or account for households caught under the bombs.

The fresh allegations land while Yemen's recognised government has been reshuffling ministers and officers after Houthi gains, and while southern factions press for a larger share of power. Independent confirmation of every casualty claim is hard in active war zones, but the family's account adds to pressure for clearer rules of engagement and public investigations when homes are hit.

title: Ukraine greets US midterm blow to Trump with cautious hope
summary: Democratic gains raise talk of a harder line in peace talks as Russia's war on Ukraine nears its fifth year.
body:
In Ukraine, the Democratic surge in the US midterms has mixed guarded optimism with dark humour about what comes next for a war drifting toward its fifth year.

Many officials and analysts think a Congress less aligned with Donald Trump could stiffen American support and change the leverage in any peace track with Moscow. Others warn that foreign policy still sits heavily with the White House, so battlefield aid and diplomacy may shift only slowly.

Kyiv has spent months reading every signal from Washington on weapons, sanctions and talks involving Kremlin envoys. A weaker Republican hand on Capitol Hill is seen as room to argue for sustained pressure on Russia rather than a rapid deal that freezes lines on Moscow's terms.

Nothing about the vote ends the fighting. Russian strikes continue and Ukrainian forces still need munitions, air defence and money. But for a public exhausted by attrition, the midterm map is being read as a possible brake on any rush to settle on unfavourable ground.

title: Europe still sees Trump as decisive on Ukraine Iran and NATO
summary: Democratic midterm wins bring private relief in some capitals, yet leaders expect the White House to keep steering the hardest foreign files.
body:
European governments are treating the Democratic midterm wave as important but not decisive for the wars and alliances that matter most to them.

Private relief is real in some ministries that feared unchecked Republican control would shrink support for Ukraine or unsettle NATO planning. Official glee is scarce. Diplomats note that Donald Trump still runs foreign policy day to day, including files on Ukraine, Iran and the future of the alliance.

Capitals are gaming out how a hostile Congress might constrain spending, appointments and sanctions while the president courts bilateral deals. Ukraine's ammunition needs, Iran contingency planning after months of strikes, and burden sharing inside NATO all still run through White House choices more than committee rooms.

The working assumption in many European briefings is continuity with sharper legislative friction, not a sudden handoff of strategy. Allies will keep talking to both parties, hedge their own defence budgets, and watch whether midterm politics hardens or softens America's next moves abroad.

title: Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production next year
summary: The company plans to free Texas factory space for driverless Cybercab builds after years of delays and weak Cybertruck sales.
body:
Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas plant next year to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis. He did not say whether the angular pickup would vanish entirely or move elsewhere, but the project's lead engineer wrote that the truck lived on through the Cybercab.

The vehicle won a loyal fan base yet arrived late in 2023 after long delays and has posted soft sales against hopes for America's truck market. Musk still calls it among Tesla's best products and told mourners online that the existing fleet will last for years, while agreeing the line is ending.

Public memory still includes the 2019 launch stunt when advertised unbreakable glass shattered on stage. Pre orders once looked huge; demand in showrooms never matched the myth. Shifting space toward unsupervised robotaxis fits Musk's bet that autonomy, not niche trucks, will define the next chapter.

Workers, suppliers and owners now wait for a clearer end date and for whether any Cybertruck work continues outside Texas. For Tesla the message is strategic: scarce factory capacity goes to the product Wall Street is being asked to value next.

title: West Bank settlement dates sold in Australia as produce of Israel
summary: Trade analysis finds millions of dollars of organic dates from illegal settlements shipped to Australia under an Israel origin label.
body:
Millions of dollars of food grown in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has reached Australia labelled as produce of Israel, according to a new review of trade papers.

Researchers at the rights group Global Echo examined commercial documents and official statistics and say at least five million US dollars of organic dates from settlements moved to Australia over eight years. Of 132 agricultural shipments from Israel studied between 2018 and 2026, 85 contained settlement goods. In 2025 and early 2026 the share was higher still, with most date consignments tied to settlement farms.

Sites named in the work include Netiv Hagdud, Beit Haarava, Arvot Jericho, Hamra, Tomer, Mechora and Naaran, areas Australia recognises as part of Palestine. Israeli rules generally require exports from settlements to be marked as Israeli unless the destination bans that practice. Australia has no ban on settlement imports and no rule forcing labels that show occupied origin.

Foreign minister Penny Wong has called the settlements illegal and urged Israel to rein in settler violence, while resisting a blanket import ban over worries for Australian firms. Campaigners say shoppers buying Israeli labelled dates may still be funding the settlement economy, and that unclear origin marking is a pattern also seen on routes into Europe.

title: Silicon Valley elites rethink politics after midterm backlash
summary: AI executives and tech donors who aligned with Donald Trump are plotting a new political strategy after that wager soured at the ballot box.
body:
Silicon Valley elites and artificial intelligence executives are redrawing their political playbook after an alliance with Donald Trump backfired in the midterm elections.

Heavy campaign spending and public alignment with the White House failed to deliver the outcomes many founders and investors sought. Voters in key races punished candidates tied to tech money and to the costs of the AI buildout, leaving donors who bet on Trump facing a Congress and state houses less friendly to unconstrained data centre expansion.

Industry figures now talk of quieter lobbying, broader bipartisan outreach and messaging that softens the industry's association with one party. Some want to stress jobs and innovation rather than culture war fights; others simply want to avoid becoming the face of another losing ticket.

The recalibration matters because AI capital and chip supply chains still depend on federal permits, power policy and export rules. After the midterms, political permission looks scarcer than venture funding. How quickly Valley leaders can rebuild credibility with both parties will shape the next round of regulation and the industry's social licence to keep building at speed.

title: Putin orders seizure of Japan Tobacco's Russian business
summary: The Kremlin move against the largest cigarette company in the Russian market further strains already frosty ties between Moscow and Tokyo.
body:
Vladimir Putin has ordered the seizure of Japan Tobacco's Russian operations, striking the largest cigarette company in that market and deepening the chill between Moscow and Tokyo.

Japan Tobacco has been a major foreign consumer brand still operating in Russia years into the war in Ukraine. Taking the business into state hands fits a wider pattern of asset transfers targeting firms from countries aligned against the Kremlin. For Tokyo the step lands as another economic and political affront after years of sanctions, diplomatic freezes and territorial disputes that never thawed.

Investors and remaining foreign companies will read the order as a fresh warning that even large, long established consumer franchises are not insulated from political retaliation. Japanese officials are likely to protest, but practical recourse inside Russia is thin once a presidential seizure order is signed.

The episode adds to Western and allied corporate exits and forced takeovers that have remade Russia's consumer landscape since 2022. For Moscow it asserts control and punishes a G7 economy. For Japan Tobacco staff and distributors on the ground it means an abrupt change of ownership with little clarity on compensation or future brand management.

title: A Trump Putin meeting in China would test Xi's balancing act
summary: Hosting the two leaders could lift Beijing's diplomatic stature, yet talks on Ukraine's future and nuclear limits would force awkward choices on China.
body:
A possible summit in China between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin would hand Xi Jinping a high profile diplomatic stage while confronting Beijing with uncomfortable decisions on Ukraine and nuclear arms limits.

Bringing the US and Russian presidents together on Chinese soil would showcase Xi as an indispensable broker when great power diplomacy is fragmented. That prestige would signal China can convene rivals others struggle to seat at the same table.

The agenda would be harder. Any serious discussion of Ukraine's future risks dragging China off its carefully managed posture of rhetorical neutrality and economic engagement with both sides. Nuclear limits talks likewise touch Chinese modernisation plans and Beijing's refusal to join US Russian style arms control that freezes a balance favourable to Washington and Moscow.

Officials in Beijing would weigh pageantry against policy traps. A summit that merely produces optics could still elevate Xi. One that forces public positions on territorial settlements or warhead ceilings could box China into commitments it has long avoided. How far Trump and Putin push those files, and how Xi responds, will show whether the meeting is a prestige win or a strategic bind.

title: Herzog to name coalition candidate by Sunday after Eisenkot leads endorsements
summary: Sixty seven lawmakers backed former military chief Gadi Eisenkot against 46 for Benjamin Netanyahu, but Israel's president says mutual vetoes still cloud who can actually form a government.
body:
Israel's president Isaac Herzog says he will name a candidate to form the next government by Sunday, after a majority of lawmakers endorsed opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Herzog spoke on Thursday after marathon consultations with parties elected to the 120 seat Knesset. Some 67 lawmakers recommended Eisenkot, a former military chief, while 46 backed Netanyahu. In televised remarks he cautioned that although the consultation numbers look clear, mutual vetoes between and within blocs make it hard to say who has the best chance of assembling a stable coalition. He plans further personal talks with party leaders over the Israeli weekend and a decision on Sunday.

October's election left neither camp with an obvious majority. Netanyahu's Likud took the most seats of any single party with 27, yet his wider religious nationalist coalition finished on 53. Eisenkot's alliance of four Jewish led parties spanning centre left to right won 48. Two parties representing Israel's Palestinian minority together took a record 19 seats.

Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out a formal government with the Arab led parties. Both of those parties nonetheless recommended him, giving him the endorsement of a comfortable majority of lawmakers. His Yashar party said 67 recommendations were the most any candidate had received since 2015 and urged Herzog to hand him the mandate quickly so he could build a national emergency government.

Netanyahu suffered a further setback when United Torah Judaism, a longtime ultra Orthodox ally, declined to recommend anyone, breaking with him over the failure to pass legislation exempting ultra Orthodox men from military service. Allies of Eisenkot argue that party's support could still be won with the right offer, leaving Netanyahu with little realistic path to a majority.

Once nominated, a candidate has 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14 day extension. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a coalition is sworn in or fresh elections are called if every attempt fails. He has seized on an election officials' inquiry into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the result, accusing Arab led parties of stealing the vote, claims critics say are meant to undermine a defeat he denies.

title: US judge pauses Trump triumphal arch works in Washington DC
summary: District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered a 14 day halt on the roughly 76 metre arch project after planning commissioners approved it over strong public opposition.
body:
A United States federal judge has ordered a temporary block on construction of President Donald Trump's planned triumphal arch in Washington DC.

US District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Friday imposed a 14 day pause on any work on the roughly 250 foot (76 metre) structure, even though the administration had said building could start as soon as Thursday. The National Capital Planning Commission held a nine hour hearing the day before and voted 8 to 4 to approve the arch despite dozens of witnesses who opposed it.

Lawsuits challenging the project include one filed in February by a group of Vietnam war veterans. Trump has proposed siting the arch near Arlington National Cemetery, prompting concern that it could interrupt the carefully designed line of sight between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Veterans argued in court papers that the vista was meant to symbolise national unity after the Civil War.

Trump first floated the arch last year to mark 250 years of US independence, comparing it to famous European arches such as the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. Critics have mocked the scheme as an Arc de Trump. It is one of several Washington projects he has pushed; on Friday he also signed a proclamation designating the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument.

Many of his capital plans have already been blocked by judges. After Democrats won control of Congress in this week's midterms, further projects are expected to face sharper scrutiny. For now the arch sits under a short court pause while litigation continues.

title: Israel tightens rules on Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem
summary: Around 180 teachers face the loss of entry permits when they expire at the end of the 2026 to 27 academic year, while funding for new schools is tied to adopting the Israeli curriculum.
body:
Palestinian education in East Jerusalem is under mounting pressure as Israel restricts teacher entry permits and links school funding to adoption of the Israeli curriculum.

About 180 Palestinian teachers have been told their travel permits into East Jerusalem will not be renewed when they expire at the end of the 2026 to 27 academic year. Many commute daily from the occupied West Bank through Israeli checkpoints. Even when permits are issued they are tightly limited by hours and location: holders may not exceed set times, may not go anywhere except the school, and since the Gaza war began in 2023 have been barred from accompanying students on trips or visiting Al Aqsa for prayer.

Permit delays already disrupted this year. Documents arrived only on 15 September, two weeks after term began, and similar delays in January triggered school strikes meant to show a united front. Teachers were also blocked from entering Jerusalem for a full week during the recent Jewish holiday of Sukkot.

Wider policies sit under a government plan framed as reducing socioeconomic gaps in East Jerusalem, whose population remains majority Palestinian despite settlement growth. Roughly half the education budget under that plan goes toward expanding teaching of the Israeli curriculum. New state funded schools must adopt that curriculum as a condition of opening, which rights monitors describe as pressure on schools and parents to abandon the Palestinian programme. Teacher training inside the Israeli education system is being expanded alongside those incentives.

An Israeli human rights organisation, Ir Amim, has warned that the measures exploit genuine educational needs to erode Palestinian educational autonomy and national identity. A separate law barring employment of teachers with degrees from Palestinian universities is expected to deepen an already severe staffing shortage.

East Jerusalem, like the West Bank, is occupied Palestinian territory under international law, though Israel treats it as part of a unified capital under its control. Teachers who have spent decades crossing checkpoints say the latest permit cuts may finally force them out of classrooms they have staffed for years, accelerating a shift toward Israeli supervised schooling in the eastern half of the city.

title: Lebanese stock food and pack bags amid fears of another Israeli push
summary: Residents who lived through earlier rounds of fighting say drones and detonations never fully stopped, and many are preparing for a possible third intensification since 2024.
body:
Lebanese families who endured earlier Israeli offensives are stocking medicine and food, charging devices and packing bags as fears grow of another escalation in the south.

A ceasefire announced in April eased the heaviest fighting after a surge of attacks that killed hundreds in a short span, yet residents say drones and distant detonations remain part of daily life. In recent weeks worry has sharpened around a potential third Israeli intensification since 2024, especially among people who lived through the autumn 2024 and March to April 2026 campaigns.

One woman from Abbasiyeh in southern Lebanon said her family prepared extra medication for her grandparents in case a new round makes supplies hard to reach. She stayed through the March intensification even when a neighbour's house was hit, but now says she would leave rather than endure another displacement. Others keep go bags ready and electronics charged should strikes resume.

Hezbollah and Israel have been at war since October 2023. Lebanese health authorities put the death toll in Lebanon at around 9,000, mostly during the major escalations. Israel invaded during each offensive and has since held territory up to about 10 kilometres inside Lebanon behind what it calls a Yellow Line, continuing demolition of towns and villages below that line and leaving border areas barely habitable.

A US brokered framework agreed in June sketched pilot zones in which Israeli forces would pull back and the Lebanese army would move in to disarm Hezbollah. Active fighting has eased since then, though Israel continues attacks and destruction in the far south. People living above the Yellow Line are mostly outside the heaviest fire but still hear constant explosions and drones and sometimes struggle to reach their land.

Reports that Washington has considered another round of strikes on Iran, coordinated with Israel, have raised questions about whether Hezbollah might resume its own attacks. Israeli officials have also accused the Lebanese army of failing its part of the framework deal, a charge the army denies. Analysts say such claims can serve as political cover for a fresh bombing campaign. For residents, the practical response is simpler: pack, stock up, and decide whether to stay or go if the sky lights up again.

title: Satellite images point to major building work near Iran missile sites
summary: Analysts say November imagery shows digging and new structures at bases near Tehran and further north, plus repairs at other military complexes hit in earlier US and Israeli strikes.
body:
Satellite imagery from November points to major new construction and repair work near Iranian missile facilities, according to analysts who reviewed the photographs.

Digging and fresh buildings are visible at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near Tehran and at the Shahroud base in the north. A British intelligence firm, MAIAR, examined the pictures and described the activity as significant. Separate imagery suggests repair work at at least a dozen other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases.

At Kermanshah in western Iran, near the Iraqi border, new roofs appear on buildings previously destroyed. At the Parchin complex east of the capital, damaged structures and debris have been cleared. Analysts also say substantial work has been finished at the Taleghan 2 facility inside Parchin, with damaged buildings levelled and an underground bunker reinforced with concrete after earlier attacks.

Excavation near Shahroud may relate to missile production, a former CIA analyst focused on Iran told reviewers. Because the nearby air base has been struck repeatedly in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps is likely seeking ways to shift production underground. A MAIAR analyst said Iran has a pattern of moving infrastructure below ground to shield it from further strikes. Defence analysts note that underground sites also make it harder for outside observers to judge how much capacity remains intact.

At Karaj, vehicles appear in the imagery and improvements seem under way at the nearby air base. One research analyst described what looks like a new portal for an underground facility. An intelligence firm analyst argued the work is unlikely to be staged merely to deceive foreign agencies, calling such a project costly for little gain.

The pictures land after White House claims that US and Israeli strikes heavily depleted Iranian forces, including Pentagon assertions that much of Iran's drone, ballistic missile and naval industrial base was destroyed. Tehran insists it still holds large missile stockpiles, and state television this week aired footage it said showed dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran.

Speculation has grown that Washington could resume attacks after this week's midterms, though Vice President JD Vance linked the war's unpopularity with voters to the Republicans' weak showing and possible loss of Senate control.

title: Trump declares the Oval Office a national monument
summary: President Donald Trump has signed an executive order making the Oval Office and some nearby rooms a national monument, aiming to lock in his gold heavy redesign and the East Wing ballroom works against later presidents.
body:
President Donald Trump has signed an executive order declaring the Oval Office, and some surrounding rooms, a national monument in a bid to stop future presidents from undoing his changes to the West Wing.

The move follows a highly visible redesign that filled the Oval Office with gold accents and a broader project that tore into the East Wing to make space for a large ballroom. Critics have already challenged parts of that building work in court, and Congress never gave a clear green light for the scale of the renovation. By wrapping the rooms in monument status, the White House is trying to raise the legal bar for anyone who wants to strip the decor back out.

The order is not an absolute freeze. It still lets a sitting president redecorate, swap furnishings and make security modifications so long as those changes do not substantially impair the historic structure. In practice that leaves room for taste and security upgrades while aiming to block a wholesale reversal of Trump's imprint.

Monument designations are normally used for landscapes, battlefields and cultural sites of lasting public value. Applying the tool to working rooms inside the White House is unusual and will invite fresh lawsuits from preservation groups and political opponents who say the president is using heritage law as a shield for personal style.

Allies cast the order as protection for a restored grandeur they say visitors and history will remember. Detractors call it an attempt to constitutionalise one administration's aesthetic after midterm losses that already weaken Trump's hand with Congress.

The practical test will come later. A future president who wants a plainer Oval Office will have to argue that new furnishings or a different colour scheme leave the historic fabric intact, or else spend political capital trying to unwind the designation. For now the public facts are clear enough: the Oval Office and named adjoining spaces sit under a new monument order, the ballroom project remains contested, and the White House insists day to day working changes are still allowed.

title: Iran security chief meets Putin and delivers a letter from Mojtaba Khamenei
summary: Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei has met Vladimir Putin in Moscow and handed over a message from Mojtaba Khamenei. Talks covered regional security, post war arrangements and plans for Russian gas pipelines into Iran.
body:
Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei has met President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and delivered a written message from Mojtaba Khamenei, deepening a wartime channel between Tehran and the Kremlin.

Public accounts of the visit say the agenda spanned regional security, arrangements after the fighting and energy cooperation, including ideas for gas pipelines that would carry Russian supply into Iran. The trip had been mapped out about a month earlier and was delayed by the military situation before Rezaei finally travelled.

The timing matters. On Wednesday Mojtaba Khamenei stated that Iran has no inclination toward submission to the United States, a line that sets a hard tone for any parallel diplomacy while his envoy sits with Putin. Moscow has already been linked in leaked material to military industrial help for Tehran; a face to face security meeting plus a personal letter raises the political signal without spelling out what was asked or promised.

Energy is the commercial half of the story. Iran wants more secure fuel and transit options while Gulf shipping stays disrupted. Russia wants markets and leverage. Pipeline talk therefore doubles as a wartime partnership marker even if construction timelines remain opaque.

Western capitals will read the Moscow stop as proof that Tehran is shopping for sponsors rather than folding under American pressure. Iranian hardliners will read it as validation that resistance still has a great power audience. The verified public record for now is narrower: Rezaei met Putin, carried a letter from Mojtaba Khamenei, discussed security and post war planning, and put gas pipelines on the table after a delay forced by the battlefield.

title: White House denies Hegseth and Rubio will quit after midterm losses
summary: The White House says Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are staying put after Republican defeats. Calls to replace Hegseth over the Iran war and rumours of a Rubio exit for 2028 have both been brushed aside.
body:
The White House has rejected claims that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are about to leave office after Republican losses in the midterm elections.

Media reports have described mounting pressure to replace Hegseth over his handling of the Iran war. An outgoing Republican lawmaker has threatened to force an impeachment vote as early as next week, and Hegseth has released a video defending his record. Officials insist he retains the president's confidence and will remain at the Pentagon.

Rubio has separately denied that he is stepping aside to prepare a 2028 presidential run. He says his plan is to keep working for President Donald Trump until the end of the term. The White House and the State Department have labelled exit rumours about him as fake news.

The denials land in a raw political climate. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have both been blamed, including by voices inside their own party, for tying the Iran conflict to the midterm defeat and to Democratic control of the House. Cabinet stability is now part of the argument over whether the administration doubles down or resets.

For allies and adversaries watching Washington, the message is meant to be continuity: the war cabinet stays, diplomacy stays with Rubio, and talk of an early scramble for 2028 is premature. For critics in Congress the opposite reading applies: that midterm punishment has not yet produced personnel consequences at the top of defence and foreign policy.

Unless resignations are announced, the public position is unchanged. Hegseth remains defence secretary, Rubio remains secretary of state, impeachment talk from a departing member is a threat rather than a concluded process, and the White House calls speculation about both men leaving a fiction.

title: Settlers set fire to Palestinian olive trees near Ramallah
summary: Israeli settlers ignited Palestinian olive trees in the village of Burqa near Ramallah, farmers say, while Israeli forces stopped them from putting out the flames.
body:
Palestinian farmers in the village of Burqa, near Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, say Israeli settlers set fire to their olive trees and that Israeli forces prevented them from extinguishing the blaze.

Olive groves are a livelihood and a seasonal clock for West Bank communities. Fires timed around harvest weeks destroy not only a year's crop but trees that take long periods to mature, amplifying the economic shock. Residents described watching flames move through the grove while being blocked from bringing water or basic firefighting tools to bear.

Settler attacks on farmland, livestock and homes are a recurring complaint logged by local councils and rights monitors. When security forces are accused of stopping Palestinian owners from defending their own trees, the grievance shifts from private violence to alleged official interference.

The Burqa incident adds to a tense West Bank picture already marked by demolitions and political deadlock in Israel after an inconclusive election. For the families involved the immediate needs are blunt: contain any remaining fire risk, count destroyed trees and document losses for later claims.

Publicly confirmed details remain short. Settlers are accused of starting the fire in a Burqa olive grove, farmers say troops stopped extinguishing efforts, and the village sits near Ramallah. Broader casualty or arrest figures were not part of the early public account.

title: Turkish parliament ratifies Mecca defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
summary: Turkey's parliament has approved the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan by 279 votes to 119. The treaty includes a collective defence clause that can be invoked if a member is attacked.
body:
Turkey's parliament has ratified the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, locking in a collective defence pledge that could draw Ankara deeper into Gulf security crises.

Lawmakers voted 279 in favour and 119 against, with 398 of the 592 seat chamber taking part. The pact was signed in August and sent to parliament last month. Its first article commits the parties to use all necessary means against threats to territorial integrity and can be triggered if a member state is attacked.

The timing is pointed. Saudi Arabia has faced repeated missile and drone assaults from Yemen's Houthis while the wider war with Iran keeps Red Sea and Gulf energy routes on edge. Ratification in Ankara lays political groundwork for further Turkish involvement if Riyadh calls for help under the new framework.

For Turkey the deal sits alongside a broader push to sit at the centre of Muslim world security diplomacy. For Pakistan it deepens a triangular military relationship that already includes training and hardware ties. For Saudi Arabia it adds another formal partner beyond traditional Western channels at a moment when air defences and deterrence messaging matter daily.

Opposition votes against the text show the step is not cost free at home. Collective defence can become an open door to deployments, logistics support or joint operations far from Turkish soil if the clause is invoked. Supporters answer that shared threats from militias and regional spillover leave little room for sitting out.

The public facts are straightforward. The Mecca agreement is now ratified in Turkey, the vote margin is clear, and the collective defence language is on the books. Whether and how it is used if Houthi or other attacks intensify will decide if the treaty stays symbolic or becomes operational.

title: Trump warns America may have to destroy the rest of Iran
summary: President Donald Trump says the United States may have to destroy what remains of Iran and that rebuilding would take 25 years, telling the public people will know soon enough if he moves. The threat lands as nuclear ideas still circulate through Qatar.
body:
President Donald Trump has warned that the United States may have to destroy the rest of Iran, saying reconstruction would take a generation and that the public will know soon enough if he acts.

The remark, reported overnight in live coverage of the conflict, sharpens the choice facing Washington after midterm losses that many Republicans themselves tie to the war. Trump has already said the fighting ends when he decides, while still insisting he does not regret the joint campaign with Israel that began in late February. His latest wording goes further: it frames a possible widening of force against Iranian territory, not only a return to the tempo of earlier strikes.

Diplomacy has not gone quiet. Public accounts say Iran has sent a nuclear proposal through Qatari mediators for Washington to study, even as Tehran waits on a set of demands it first laid out in condensed form this autumn. Officials have described concrete nuclear ideas under review, yet no verified text of enrichment limits, sanctions relief or inspection steps has been released. That gap leaves markets and allies guessing whether a bargain or a new escalation comes first.

The warning also lands against a hard commercial backdrop. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains tightly constrained, tanker incidents continue to feed insurance nerves, and fuel prices at home were cited by Trump himself as a reason some voters walked away. Destroy rhetoric raises the political cost of another round even as it signals resolve to audiences who want the war finished on American terms.

For now the public facts are limited but stark. The president has floated destroying what is left of Iran, tied any move to a 25 year rebuild, and left the timing opaque. Whether the next step is a deal on Qatar's channel or a fresh military order remains the central unanswered question of the week.

title: Trump says a Russia Ukraine deal is very close after meeting Putin's envoy
summary: President Donald Trump says agreement with Russia on Ukraine is very close after hosting Kirill Dmitriev at the White House. He offered no details and did not meet a visiting Ukrainian delegation the same day.
body:
President Donald Trump says a deal to end the Russia Ukraine war is very close after he met Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy linked to Vladimir Putin, at the White House.

Trump gave no concrete terms. He suggested the understanding could reach beyond Ukraine and touch all of Europe, a phrase that immediately fuelled speculation about security guarantees, sanctions relief or territorial arrangements without confirming any of them. He did not meet a Ukrainian delegation that was also in Washington around the same time.

The encounter followed a separate track led by Melania Trump, who hosted Russian and Ukrainian representatives to mark a localised truce around Oleshky. That pause, lasting from 27 October to 1 November, allowed roughly 800 civilians to leave the Russian occupied town in Kherson region. The first lady's channel was presented as a humanitarian opening; the president's meeting with Dmitriev is being sold as the political follow through.

Sceptics note that previous Trump claims of imminent breakthroughs have come and gone while fighting continues. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned against any settlement that freezes occupation lines without Kyiv's consent. Russian envoys, for their part, tend to press for recognition of battlefield gains and limits on Ukraine's future alliances.

What is verified today is limited but notable. Trump met Dmitriev, called a deal very close, floated a scope larger than Ukraine alone, skipped the Ukrainian visitors, and did so days after Melania's Oleshky humanitarian window closed. Whether those strands produce a text that both Moscow and Kyiv will sign remains the unanswered test.

title: Nithya Raman wins Los Angeles mayor's race
summary: Progressive councillor Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Karen Bass and is set to become the city's first South Asian mayor. She pledged action on homelessness, housing and the police leadership.
body:
Nithya Raman, a progressive Los Angeles city councillor, has defeated incumbent mayor Karen Bass and is on course to become the first South Asian to lead America's second largest city.

Results called on Thursday put Raman on about 52 percent. The 45 year old, born in India and trained as an urban planner, overcame endorsements for Bass from California governor Gavin Newsom, former vice president Kamala Harris and former House speaker Nancy Pelosi. Her campaign drew backing from the Democratic Socialists of America, part of a wider midterm surge in which that movement claimed a role in hundreds of candidacies and ballot fights.

Raman had once endorsed Bass's re election before reversing course and filing just before the February deadline. In her victory speech she promised a more ambitious city, more affordable housing, better basic services and a different approach to homelessness that puts more medical teams with people living on the street. She also called for replacing the police chief over concerns about cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in more than two decades to lose a re election bid. Her term was dogged by criticism of the homelessness crisis and of the response to the deadly Palisades Fire, which began while she was overseas. In a statement she congratulated Raman and pledged a smooth transition, recalling her own historic win four years ago as the city's first Black woman mayor.

Raman inherits a city of more than 3.8 million people and the approaching 2028 Olympic Games. Delivery on housing and street homelessness will decide whether the progressive wave that lifted her, and earlier lifted New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, can govern at metropolitan scale.

title: Young voters and Gen Z winners reshape the midterm map
summary: Melat Kiros becomes the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress as younger Americans swung hard to Democrats. About seven in ten voters under 30 backed Democratic House candidates.
body:
The 2026 midterms marked a visible shift in who holds power in Washington, with Melat Kiros becoming the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress and younger voters swinging sharply toward Democrats.

Kiros, a 29 year old Ethiopian born democratic socialist from Colorado, won the Denver area House seat after upsetting long serving Democrat Diana DeGette in the primary. She joins Florida's Maxwell Frost, the first Gen Z House member elected in 2022. Of 117 Generation Z candidates who sought Congress this year, 24 reached the general election ballot, according to the Future Caucus group.

National polling of voters showed about seven in ten people under 30 backed the Democratic House candidate, against about three in ten for Republicans. That is a sharp reverse from 2024, when the youngest cohort split roughly evenly between Donald Trump and Kamala Harris. First time midterm voters, who skew young, also leaned Democratic. Their absolute weight was limited: only about one in ten midterm voters were under 30. Anger still stood out. Roughly half of young voters said they were angry about the country's direction, and about six in ten under 30 said opposing Trump was a reason for their House vote.

Those shifts helped Democrats flip Senate seats in states including Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina. Kiros's platform, from Medicare for All to ending what she called genocide in Palestine and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, signals how far left some of the new cohort sits from older party leaders.

The story is not only age. It is a pipeline of first time candidates who beat incumbents and then rode a youth backlash against the White House. Whether that cohort can move legislation, or remains a loud minority inside a larger Democratic majority, will define the next two years.

title: Israeli demolitions in Biddu leave more than 100 people homeless
summary: Israeli forces demolished five homes in Biddu in the occupied West Bank, residents say, displacing more than a hundred Palestinians. Locals say the raid came without warning after legal efforts failed to stop it.
body:
Israeli forces have demolished five homes in the village of Biddu, northwest of Jerusalem in the occupied West Bank, displacing more than 100 Palestinians, according to residents and video news reports.

Ahmad Abu Eid, a Biddu resident, said troops raided the town without warning even after families tried to block the demolitions through legal channels. The loss of five houses in a single operation leaves extended families without shelter at the start of winter and adds to a wider pattern of home demolitions across the West Bank that rights groups monitor week by week.

Biddu sits in a sensitive belt northwest of Jerusalem where settlement expansion, road barriers and permit rules already squeeze Palestinian building. When homes come down faster than courts can freeze orders, the practical result is sudden displacement and pressure on relatives to absorb whole households.

The demolitions land in a charged political week in Israel, with President Isaac Herzog still hearing party leaders after an election that left Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot short of a clear majority. West Bank policy is often a fault line between those camps and the Arab majority parties now courted as kingmakers.

For the families in Biddu the national coalition maths are remote. Their immediate needs are shelter, storage of salvaged belongings and a paper trail for any later claim. The public record so far is the five homes destroyed, the resident account of a sudden raid, and a displacement toll above one hundred people.

title: Saudi led coalition says it downed a missile aimed at Medina region
summary: Coalition air defences destroyed a ballistic missile fired by Yemen's Houthis toward the Medina region, officials say. Civil defence had just warned of danger near the oil port of Yanbu, which the Houthis deny targeting as a holy city.
body:
The Saudi led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis says its air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired toward the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest cities.

Coalition spokesman Turki al Malki announced the interception on Thursday minutes after Saudi civil defence warned of potential danger near the strategic Red Sea port of Yanbu. The early warning platform later said the threat had passed. Yanbu is a major oil export hub and a key outlet for crude moved across the kingdom on the East West pipeline, a route that has mattered more since the wider war with Iran disrupted Gulf shipping.

The Houthis rejected any suggestion they were aiming at Medina itself. Military spokesman Yahya Saree called that claim a blatant falsehood and said Houthi operations target only oil facilities and military bases. The group has struck Yanbu and other Saudi airports, energy sites and bases repeatedly in recent months, disrupting air traffic and keeping civil defence on alert.

On the ground inside Yemen, the internationally recognised government claimed fresh gains around Sanamat in Taiz governorate and said its forces carried out more than a thousand targeting operations in a day. Those kill and destruction figures have not been independently verified. Analysts at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies describe a war of attrition that is increasingly tied to the wider regional confrontation with Iran rather than to Yemen's internal balance alone.

The Medina region alert will resonate far beyond the battlefield. Any missile track near Islam's second holiest city raises the political temperature even when interceptors succeed. For Riyadh the episode underlines why Yanbu and the pipeline corridor remain priority targets to defend. For the Houthis the denial is an attempt to separate attacks on energy and military sites from the charge of menacing a sacred city.

title: Newsom commutes every death sentence on California's row
summary: Governor Gavin Newsom has turned all 548 death sentences into life without parole in a largely symbolic move in a state that has not executed anyone since 2006. He called state killing incompatible with California's values.
body:
California governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on the state's death row to life in prison without the possibility of parole, emptying the largest condemned population in the United States.

In a letter he argued that state sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the legal system and diminishes everyone it touches. He said the death penalty has failed by every measure, cannot be applied fairly, and has put innocent people at risk. Life without parole, he wrote, is the harshest penalty the state can lawfully and ethically enforce.

The step is largely symbolic in practice. California has not executed a prisoner since 2006, and only 13 people have been put to death since voters restored capital punishment in 1978. Newsom already imposed a moratorium in 2019. Experts say commuting the row could still save millions of dollars a year in litigation costs. He acknowledged the decision will anger and hurt some victims' families and said that burden would weigh on him alone.

Politically the timing is pointed. Newsom is term limited and winding down his final months, with fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra projected to succeed him after this week's midterms. The governor has been discussed as a possible 2028 presidential contender, and a blanket clemency on capital punishment will become part of that national audition whether he seeks it or not.

For the prisoners the change means obscurity rather than a lethal chamber. For California it closes a chapter that courts, governors and voters have fought over for decades, replacing the threat of execution with permanent imprisonment.

title: US midterm shock hardens the fight over who leads Israel
summary: Republican losses in America are feeding Israel's coalition struggle, as rivals say Benjamin Netanyahu's brand has become a political liability in Washington. Arab majority parties say they will back Gadi Eisenkot for prime minister.
body:
The scale of Republican losses in the US midterms is spilling directly into Israel's race to form a government, weakening Benjamin Netanyahu's claim that he alone can lock in American support.

Early American post mortems have focused on the war with Iran and on ties to Israel, themes Vice President JD Vance himself highlighted. Opposition figures in Israel argue that Netanyahu's record, including the Gaza war, the Iran conflict and regional strikes, has made Israel a harder sell in US politics. Former prime minister Yair Lapid stressed his own links on Capitol Hill and said US voters were reacting against extreme ministers, settler violence and Netanyahu personally more than against Israel as such.

Avigdor Lieberman went further, suggesting President Donald Trump's election day talk of ending US military aid was the price of an endorsement for Netanyahu, citing an annual figure of 3.8 billion dollars. Security analyst Ahron Bregman warned that if American money stops, Israel's defence burden, already about 7 percent of GDP, will rise and households will feel it.

On the numbers, Netanyahu's right wing bloc has 53 seats, eight short of a majority. Eisenkot's opposition bloc has 48, while Ra'am and the Joint List hold 19 between them and have said they will support Eisenkot for prime minister. Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have rejected a unity deal with Netanyahu, leaving President Isaac Herzog to choose who gets the first mandate.

For many Israelis the fear is simpler: that automatic bipartisan cover in Washington has thinned. How Herzog reads that mood, and whether Eisenkot can turn outside Arab party backing into a workable arrangement, will decide whether the midterm shock becomes a decisive argument against another Netanyahu term.

title: Trump civil rights chief resigns as Congress turns hostile
summary: Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon has left the Justice Department, the first senior Trump official to quit since the midterms. Democrats preparing to take charge of Congress are expected to dig into the civil rights division's record.
body:
Harmeet Dhillon has resigned as assistant attorney general for civil rights, becoming the first senior Trump administration official to step down since Democrats swept the midterms.

Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed he had accepted her resignation, praising her for defending civil liberties and enforcing the law without fear or favour. Dhillon, a close Trump ally confirmed in April 2025, oversaw a sweeping remake of the Justice Department division that enforces anti discrimination rules. Hundreds of former department officials wrote last December that the division was being destroyed under Trump.

Her exit lands as the incoming Democratic Congress prepares investigations into immigration agent shootings and into the handling of Jeffrey Epstein related files, areas that sit uncomfortably close to civil rights and accountability fights. Losing the division's public face before those probes begin may be an attempt to get ahead of subpoenas, or simply the first of several departures as the political ground shifts.

Whatever the private motive, the public signal is clear. After a campaign season that punished the White House, the administration is starting to lose top lawyers who drove its most contentious legal agenda. Democrats now have both the votes and a named vacancy to argue that civil rights enforcement needs a reset.

For career staff inside the division the resignation raises a practical question: who sets priorities for the next two years, and will Congress's oversight change the cases that move or stall. For Trump the risk is contagion, if other senior lawyers decide early exits beat months of hearings.

title: Melania Trump hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House
summary: The US first lady urged a more lasting truce after the Oleshky evacuation pause, bringing senior Russian and Ukrainian figures together in Washington. Both sides thanked her for a role in last week's local ceasefire.
body:
Melania Trump welcomed Russian and Ukrainian officials to the White House on Thursday and called for a more enduring ceasefire after last week's humanitarian pause around Oleshky in southern Kherson.

The White House presented the gathering as a rare moment in which a first lady personally brought representatives of two warring states into the building for diplomacy. Among those present were Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova, Ukrainian MP David Arakhamia and Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets.

Hundreds of Oleshky residents facing hunger and bombardment were able to leave during a six day local truce that Moscow and Kyiv both credited her with helping to broker. She said she had reviewed demining plans, aerial images, roads, evacuation routes, hospital access and medical resources, and hoped the episode would inspire wider peace. She handed Dmitriev and Arakhamia personal letters for their presidents and thanked both Volodymyr Zelensky and Vladimir Putin without rehearsing the origins of the full scale invasion.

Dmitriev thanked her for saving lives and gave her a framed drawing by an eleven year old evacuee. All parties conveyed gratitude from their presidents for her part in the local ceasefire, even while broader official peace talks have stalled for months.

The meeting does not itself end the war. It does keep a civilian track open at a senior symbolic level, and it ties the first lady's staff to any follow on humanitarian steps that may be attempted while soldiers keep fighting elsewhere.

title: Schumer faces a fight to keep the Senate Democratic helm
summary: Chuck Schumer says he will be elected majority leader after the Democratic midterm sweep, but at least seven incoming senators have refused to pledge him their votes. Critics want a sharper break from the Trump years.
body:
Chuck Schumer says he will return as Democratic majority leader after his party's midterm romp, yet a visible revolt among newly elected senators means the job is no longer a coronation.

The New York Democrat told reporters in Washington he would be re elected to lead the larger caucus. At least seven incoming freshmen have publicly declined to commit to him ahead of next month's leadership vote. Some want a more progressive champion for the final stretch of Donald Trump's presidency and the run into 2028. Others still resent Schumer's primary choices, including his backing of Haley Stevens over Abdul El Sayed in Michigan.

Critics also list older grievances: his emphasis on security aid to Israel, his failure to block more of Trump's cabinet, and his decision last year to support a Republican plan that reopened the government without winning key Democratic priorities such as healthcare subsidies. California governor Gavin Newsom called that a capitulation; Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib said he should have quit as leader over it.

Schumer's answer is to preview an aggressive majority agenda: investigations into the Trump administration, resistance to the president's programme, and an end to the war with Iran. Whether that package reunites the caucus will be tested in the private count that actually chooses the leader.

The irony is sharp. Democrats just delivered one of their strongest midterm showings in a generation, yet the first internal argument is about who should steer the victory. Schumer remains the favourite on experience and relationships, but the open refusals from newcomers show that a slice of the new majority wants a different face at the top.

title: Iran reports tankers hit by mines in the Strait of Hormuz
summary: Iranian forces say at least five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire after striking mines or taking damage in and near the Strait of Hormuz. The incidents deepen shipping risk on a route that usually carries about a fifth of the world's oil.
body:
Iranian military and Revolutionary Guard statements on Thursday described a string of fires on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, saying at least five oil tankers and a tugboat were damaged after striking naval mines or suffering sudden blazes.

According to the Guard, a large tanker trying to use a southern passage it called illegal hit a mine overnight, caught fire and was forced to stop. A second supertanker exiting the eastern side of the strait was halted by a major fire, and a tug that approached to fight the flames also burned. The army later said three more tankers struck mines east of the waterway in the morning and around noon and likewise caught fire.

Separately, British maritime monitors reported that a tanker was struck by two projectiles about fifty nautical miles north of Qatar late on Wednesday. The monitors did not name the ship or its flag, and no group immediately claimed that attack. A Qatari LNG carrier was also hit by unidentified objects in the Gulf last week, its operator said, with no crew injuries reported.

Traffic through the strait has been tightly restricted since the wider war with Iran began in late February. In normal times the waterway moves roughly one fifth of global oil consumption, so every fresh incident feeds freight and energy market nerves. Iranian spokesmen framed the damaged tankers as vessels that had entered unsafe or unauthorised lanes, while offering no sign that passage would become freer while fighting continues.

The timing matters politically as well as commercially. Washington is still weighing its next moves after US midterm losses that many analysts link in part to the Iran conflict, and any renewed sense that Hormuz remains mined or contested will keep pressure on insurers, shipowners and importers that depend on Gulf crude and fuel.

title: Iran reviews concrete nuclear proposals amid Qatar mediation
summary: Officials say Tehran is examining detailed ideas on its nuclear programme, a sign that Qatar led efforts to avert a wider US Iran war have gained some traction. Public details of the terms remain scarce.
body:
Iran is reviewing concrete proposals on its nuclear programme, officials say, in the clearest recent hint that mediated diplomacy is still moving even while fighting continues.

Public summaries say Tehran's willingness to re engage on nuclear questions suggests Qatar led efforts to stop a wider US Iran war have gained some traction. The actual paper has not been published. No verified list of enrichment limits, sanctions relief or inspection steps has been released with the claim that proposals are under study.

That narrow disclosure still matters. It shows a live channel exists under Qatari auspices at a moment when American politics is debating how to end the conflict and Iran wants relief from naval pressure, frozen assets and oil export curbs. Whether the review ends in a freeze, a broader bargain or another stall depends on terms that remain out of public view.

For now the record supports only this: officials describe detailed nuclear ideas on Tehran's desk, not a finished deal.

title: Herzog hears rivals as Israel seeks a path out of deadlock
summary: Israel's president is meeting party leaders after an election that left Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot both short of a majority. Arab majority parties look like kingmakers as turnout among Arab citizens surged.
body:
Israel's president Isaac Herzog is holding talks with party leaders to decide who should first try to form a government after last month's election produced no clear winner. He has urged every camp to help the country avoid another ballot.

Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition fell from 68 seats to 53 in the 120 seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot holds 48. That leaves parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, with a record 19 seats between them, as the most plausible kingmakers. The Joint List has 11 and the more conservative Ra'am has eight.

Arab Israeli turnout more than doubled to about 80 percent, reshaping the arithmetic even though Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote. Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen has said his voters want change after years of sharper racism, crime and exclusion under the outgoing coalition, while admitting deep disagreements with Eisenkot. He has described the choice as one between bad and worse rather than between good and better.

In Israel's system the president, though largely ceremonial day to day, judges which candidate has the best first chance of building a stable majority. Arab majority parties have signalled they would back Eisenkot for the premiership from outside a cabinet, even as Eisenkot's bloc has historically been wary of formal partnership with them. Netanyahu's camp remains short of 61 seats and has no obvious route without unlikely defections.

The deadlock keeps markets, allies and local voters waiting. Whoever Herzog nominates will face a narrow path: satisfy enough partners to govern, blunt claims that the result was illegitimate, and show that a working coalition can be assembled without plunging Israel straight back into another campaign.

title: AI and chip stocks slide as investors read the midterm map
summary: US markets fell sharply on Thursday with the Nasdaq leading losses as traders bet that a Democratic surge will mean tougher scrutiny of data centres and the AI boom. A one day relief rally after the vote quickly reversed.
body:
United States markets dropped on Thursday as artificial intelligence and chip shares led a broad selloff, reversing Wednesday's relief rally that followed the Democratic midterm sweep.

By midday the tech heavy Nasdaq was down about 4.8 percent, the S&P 500 about 3.6 percent and the Dow about 2.8 percent. Investors who had first welcomed limits on unilateral White House policy shocks pivoted to a different fear: that newly empowered Democrats in Congress and in the states will slow data centre building and tighten oversight of an AI industry that has driven much of the recent bull run.

That reading matches commentary from market desks and from executives who already admit the sector fuelled public hostility with its land, power and water demands. Shares linked to SpaceX and other high flying tech names were also caught in the downdraft as traders cut risk across speculative growth stories.

Politics and portfolios are now tightly braided. Democrats campaigned in part on anger at Silicon Valley influence and at the costs of the AI buildout, while heavy campaign spending by technology billionaires failed to stop the blue wave in several races. Markets that once treated AI capacity as a one way bet are repricing political permission as a scarce input.

None of this proves regulation will arrive at the speed traders fear. It does show that after the midterms, the assumption of frictionless expansion for data centres and model trainers is no longer the default on Wall Street.

title: Nusseibeh makes her case for the UN top job
summary: Lana Nusseibeh, a late entrant to succeed Antonio Guterres, says she would serve independently and put Sudan's war first. Supporters see a seasoned diplomat who can still reshape a deadlocked race.
body:
Lana Nusseibeh has entered the contest to become the next United Nations secretary general with a clear pitch: she would answer to the Charter, not to Abu Dhabi, and she would be judged by what she delivers in her first hundred days.

The 48 year old state minister of the United Arab Emirates and former ambassador in New York is a late arrival in a race that must settle before Antonio Guterres leaves at year end. She said every candidate comes from somewhere, that great and small states alike have faced UN findings on international humanitarian law, and that she would speak frankly to every government while balancing pragmatism and principle. Sudan's war and its humanitarian catastrophe would be her immediate priority.

Critics, including Sudan's military authorities, some rights groups and former Human Rights Watch director Kenneth Roth, argue she is unfit because she rebutted claims that the UAE backed the Rapid Support Forces while serving as a diplomat. Abu Dhabi denies arming that force. Her answer is to invite scrutiny of her record once in office rather than of the capital she once represented.

Supporters see a different ledger. She comes from a Palestinian family with roots in Jerusalem; her father Zaki worked as a translator to Sheikh Zayed. The Palestinian Authority and several Gulf governments have endorsed her. Diplomats who watched her in New York recall adroit floor work, and she has backed Gaza humanitarian efforts. On the Board of Peace linked to the Trump Gaza plan she frames the body as complementary to the UN and useful where the system is gridlocked.

Her vision is to restore peacemaking so the UN sits at the centre of crises rather than as a spectator. She favours sharper priorities over blunt cuts, and closer partnership with the private sector, the World Bank, the IMF and regional development banks. Criticism from President Donald Trump, she suggests, is galvanising a push for efficiency, though she has not spoken to him about her candidacy.

The politics remain open. Tradition points to a Latin American turn, with figures including Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan and Argentina's Rafael Grossi in the field, while Turkey's Volkan Sinirlioglu has entered. Washington has played down regional rotation. An unofficial Security Council straw poll put Nusseibeh fourth, with another round due later Thursday. Frontrunners face resistance among the permanent five, which is why her late bid retains room to grow.

title: Republicans weigh a new direction as Vance looks to 2028
summary: After heavy midterm losses, senior Republicans are debating how far to move away from the Trump brand. Vance is seen positioning himself for a fresh start ahead of the next presidential race.
body:
Senior Republicans are scrambling for a new course after Democrats swept both houses of Congress in this week's midterms, and much of the debate turns on how far the party can step back from President Donald Trump's brand without tearing itself apart.

Vice President JD Vance moved first. Hours after the scale of the defeat became clear, he argued on X that the war with Iran, and the strain of American ties to Israel, had driven former Trump voters to the other side. He told critics who had warned the party that they were right, and urged them to channel that energy into choosing Republicans who share their worldview. Oil markets reacted in kind: Brent crude slipped as traders judged that a weaker White House hand made a fresh round of strikes less likely.

The economic backdrop is harsh. After Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz early in the conflict, crude surged and has stayed elevated for months, feeding higher fuel and food prices at home.
